summary.title: Can giant planets form by gravitational fragmentation of discs? Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region
summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: planetary system and protoplanetary disc formation
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates whether giant planets can form close to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary discs. Two competing theories of giant planet formation are core accretion and gravitational fragmentation. Core accretion is slow, requiring millions of years, which may exceed the lifetime of circumstellar discs. Gravitational fragmentation is fast, occurring on a dynamical timescale of a few hundred years, but requires two conditions: gravitational instability (Toomre Q < 1) and fast cooling (tCOOL < C(γ) tORB). The authors use radiative hydrodynamic simulations with a newly developed method that accounts for radiative transfer effects, including the equation of state and energy equation, in smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations. They simulate a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star, extending from 2 to 40 AU, in two cases: one with a constant background radiation field of 10 K, and one with additional heating from the central star. In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, the disc cannot cool fast enough (cooling time > 2 tORB). In the second case, the disc is not gravitationally unstable (Q > 1.5). The results corroborate previous studies by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), who used different radiative transfer treatments. The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii < 50 AU. This work contributes to resolving the contradictory results in the literature about whether disc fragmentation can produce giant planets close to the central star, which stem from different treatments of radiative transfer. The study uses realistic dust opacities and an equation of state that includes the rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen, as well as the chemical states of hydrogen and helium. The simulations are performed using the SPH code dragon, which uses an octal tree to compute gravity and find neighbours, adaptive smoothing lengths, multiple particle timesteps, artificial viscosity with the Balsara switch, and a second-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme. The authors also compare their results with analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) for the vertical temperature profile of the disc. The study is important because it provides evidence that gravitational fragmentation is not a viable mechanism for forming giant planets close to the central star, which has implications for our understanding of planet formation and the diversity of exoplanets. The authors acknowledge that their results are consistent with previous simulations and analytical calculations, which suggests that the conclusion is robust. However, they also note that fragmentation may be possible at larger radii (> 100 AU), where the cooling times are sufficiently short, but that such objects are unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. The study is limited by the assumption of a constant mean molecular weight and the neglect of metal contributions, which may affect the accuracy of the results. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive investigation of the possibility of giant planet formation by gravitational fragmentation, using state-of-the-art numerical simulations and realistic physical models.

The study is limited by the assumption of a constant mean molecular weight and the neglect of metal contributions, which may affect the accuracy of the results. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive investigation of the possibility of giant planet formation by gravitational fragmentation, using state-of-the-art numerical simulations and realistic physical models.

Research Context
Disc fragmentation has been proposed as a mechanism for forming giant planets close to solar-type stars. Core accretion is slow, requiring millions of years, which may exceed the lifetime of circumstellar discs. Gravitational fragmentation is fast, occurring on a dynamical timescale of a few hundred years. Two conditions must be met for discs to fragment gravitationally: gravitational instability and fast cooling. The literature has contradictory results about whether disc fragmentation can produce giant planets close to the central star. The contradictions arise mainly from different treatments of radiative transfer in discs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether giant planets can form by gravitational fragmentation of discs in the inner region. The authors hypothesize that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii < 50 AU. The authors predict that in a disc heated by a background radiation field of 10 K, the disc will not fragment because it cannot cool fast enough. The authors predict that in a disc with additional heating from the central star, the disc will not fragment because it is not gravitationally unstable. The authors predict that their results will corroborate previous studies by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The authors predict that the disc will be Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU in the first case. The authors predict that the disc will cool fast enough to fragment at radii > 20 AU in the second case, but will not fragment because it is not gravitationally unstable. The authors predict that the disc will be stabilized by stellar heating, with no spiral arms forming.

Methodological Details
The study uses the SPH code dragon to perform the simulations. The code uses an octal tree to compute gravity and find neighbours. The code uses adaptive smoothing lengths and multiple particle timesteps. The code uses artificial viscosity with the Balsara switch. The code uses a second-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme. The energy equation is treated with the method of Stamatellos et al. (2007). The method accounts for compressional heating, viscous heating, radiation heating from the background, radiation cooling, and radiation heating from the particle's neighbourhood. The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and helium. The equation of state accounts for the rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen. The equation of state accounts for the chemical states of hydrogen and helium depending on temperature and density. The equation of state includes the effects of H2 dissociation, H0 ionisation, and the first and second ionisation of He. The temperatures in the simulations are not high enough for molecular hydrogen to dissociate.

Procedures And Architectures
The study simulates a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star. The disc initially extends from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density is Σ(R) ∼ R−1/2. The initial temperature is T(R) ∼ R−1. The disc surface profile is Σ(R) = Σ0 R−1/2, with Σ0 = 1.6 × 103 g cm−2. The disc temperature profile is Td(R) = (T0² (R/AU)−2 + T∞²)1/2. The temperature at R ≃ 1 AU is T0 = 1200 K. The asymptotic temperature far from the central star is T∞ = 10 K. The initial thickness z0(R) of the disc is calculated by balancing the vertical component of the gravitational force of the star and the gravitational force of the underlying disc against the pressure force due to the disc thermal pressure. The study performs 2 disc simulations. The first simulation uses a constant background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. The second simulation uses radiation from the central star, with TBGR ∼ R−1.

Key Results
In the first simulation, the disc relaxes to a quasi-steady state within ~250 yr. In the first simulation, the disc does not fragment despite being Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU. In the first simulation, the disc cannot cool fast enough, with the cooling time throughout the disc generally > 2 tORB. In the first simulation, the temperatures calculated are ~15% higher than those of Boley et al. (2006). In the first simulation, the temperatures calculated are less than 3% higher than those of Cai et al. (2007). In the first simulation, the results are more comparable to the results of Cai et al. (2007) with external envelope irradiation of 15 K. In the first simulation, the vertical temperature profiles are similar to those predicted by Hubeny (1990). In the second simulation, the disc remains almost constant in temperature due to heating from the central star. In the second simulation, the disc is overall hotter than in the first case due to heating from the central star. In the second simulation, the disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii > 20 AU. In the second simulation, the disc does not fragment because it is not gravitationally unstable, with Q > 1.5. In the second simulation, the disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The disc cannot cool fast enough in the first case, which prevents fragmentation. The disc is not gravitationally unstable in the second case, which prevents fragmentation. The results corroborate previous studies by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The results are consistent with previous simulations and analytical calculations. The results suggest that fragmentation is possible at larger distances (> 100 AU) from the central star. The results suggest that fragmentation at large radii produces mostly brown dwarfs and occasionally low-mass hydrogen-burning stars or planetary-mass objects. The results suggest that planetary-mass objects formed at large radii are unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. The results suggest that planetary-mass objects formed at large radii are more likely to be ejected into the field through 3-body interactions. The results suggest that gas giant planets probably cannot form close to the central star by gravitational fragmentation of discs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The temperatures in the simulations are not high enough for molecular hydrogen to dissociate. The contributions from metals are ignored, so the gas composition remains the same. The mean molecular weight µ is constant in the simulations. The temperatures calculated are ~15% higher than those of Boley et al. (2006). The discrepancies between the simulations are attributable to using a different background radiation field. The discrepancies at small radii could be due to higher viscous heating in the simulations. The Toomre parameter in the simulation is generally higher than that of Boley et al. (2006). The cooling times are lower in the simulation than in Boley et al. (2006). The spiral arms that develop in the disc are weaker than those reported by Boley et al. (2006). The temperatures calculated are generally larger than those of Boley et al. (2006).

Claims
Disc fragmentation is unlikely to be able to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii < 50 AU. The disc cannot cool fast enough in the first case. The disc is not gravitationally unstable in the second case. The results corroborate previous studies by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The disc does not fragment in both cases. Fragmentation is possible at larger distances (> 100 AU) from the central star. The disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii > 20 AU in the second case. The results suggest that fragmentation at large radii produces mostly brown dwarfs and occasionally low-mass hydrogen-burning stars or planetary-mass objects. The results suggest that planetary-mass objects formed at large radii are unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. The results suggest that planetary-mass objects formed at large radii are more likely to be ejected into the field through 3-body interactions.
The disc cannot cool fast enough in the first case, which prevents fragmentation. The cooling time throughout the disc is generally > 2 tORB. The disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU. The disc does not fragment despite being Toomre unstable. The adiabatic index is γ = 5/3 outside ~10 AU where the temperature is less than ~80 K. The maximum cooling time for the disc to fragment increases from 0.5 to 2 tORB when γ decreases from 5/3 to 7/5. The results suggest that discs are not expected to fragment within ~30 AU. The results suggest that the disc does not fragment.
The disc is not gravitationally unstable in the second case, which prevents fragmentation. The disc is overall hotter than in the first case due to heating from the central star. The disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii > 20 AU. The disc does not fragment because it is not gravitationally unstable, with Q > 1.5. The disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms. The heating from the central star stabilizes the disc. The results suggest that discs are even less prone to fragment in their inner regions when the effect of stellar irradiation is taken into account. The results agree with previous simulations of discs heated by envelope radiation.

Data And Code Availability
The computations were performed using the UK Astrophysical Fluids Facility (UKAFF). The study acknowledges support by PPARC grant PP/E000967/1.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The simulation was repeated using a smaller number of SPH particles (5 × 104). The evolution of the thermal energy, surface density, temperature, Toomre parameter and cooling time were essentially the same. The profiles change only slowly with time as the disc cools quasi-statically. The results are comparable with the results of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The disc is gravitationally unstable at R ~ 20-30 AU, but it does not fragment because it cannot cool fast enough.

Ethical Considerations
The study acknowledges useful discussions with R. Durisen, A. Boley and K. Rice.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the internal energy of the disc for a disc under low background heating (TBGR = 10 K; bottom, red line) and for a disc irradiated by the central star (TBGR(R) ∼ R−1; top, blue line). Figure 2 shows the logarithmic column density (top) and cross-section of the density on the x-z plane (bottom) for a disc heated by a low-temperature background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. Figure 4 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y plane (top) and on the x-z plane (bottom) for a disc heated by a low-temperature background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. Figure 5 shows the cooling time (in units of the local orbital period) in the x-y plane (top) and on the x-z plane (bottom) for a disc heated by a low-temperature background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. Figure 8 shows the disc temperature profiles vertically to the disc midplane at different radii from the central star (6, 10, 15, and 20 AU, top to bottom). Figure 14 shows the azimuthally averaged Toomre parameter and cooling time (in units of the local orbital period) at 5 instances the evolution of a disc heated by the central star.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is that disc fragmentation is unlikely to be able to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii < 50 AU. 2. The strongest evidence is that the disc does not fragment in both cases, because it cannot cool fast enough in the first case and it is not gravitationally unstable in the second case. 3. The future path is to investigate the possibility of giant planet formation by gravitational fragmentation at larger radii (> 100 AU), where the cooling times are sufficiently short.
